steps.title: Six stages, each one loads the next
steps.body:
A processor cannot start a program as big as Linux straight from power-on, because its main RAM is not even working yet. So boot is a chain: each stage is small, prepares something, and loads the next one.

Read the cards left to right. Red cards are the **secure world** (code the normal operating system cannot touch), blue cards are boot stages, teal is Linux. Each card says where the stage runs, what it does and what this repository builds it from. The bars at the bottom show what is still in memory once Linux is up.

steps.title: The Boot ROM is fixed in silicon and picks BL2
steps.body:
The Boot ROM is code burned into the chip. It samples the BOOT pins to choose the medium, finds the GPT (the SD card's partition table) entry named `fsbla1`, checks the STM32 header and copies BL2 into SYSRAM, the chip's 256 KiB of on-chip RAM.

Nothing here can be configured or rebuilt, which is why the partition names on the card are not negotiable: with the wrong name the ROM finds nothing to load.

steps.title: BL2 makes the big RAM work, then loads everything else
steps.body:
BL2 is the second boot stage of TF-A (Trusted Firmware-A, Arm's reference secure firmware). It runs at EL3, the most privileged CPU level, from SYSRAM `0x0E017000`.

It trains the LPDDR4 memory, sets the RISAF firewalls (hardware that restricts who may access memory regions), then reads the FIP (Firmware Image Package, one file holding the later stages) from the `fip` partition and loads BL31, OP-TEE and U-Boot. Without the DDR training nothing could be loaded into main memory.

steps.title: BL31 never leaves: it is the secure monitor
steps.body:
BL31 is the resident part of TF-A, running at EL3 from SYSRAM `0x0E000000`. Every SMC (secure monitor call, the instruction that crosses between the worlds) goes through it, and it serves PSCI, the standard interface for turning CPUs on and off and resetting.

At boot it starts OP-TEE first and then exits to U-Boot. It lives in the `fip.bin` file, built from the same `trusted-firmware-a` tree as BL2.

steps.title: OP-TEE is the secure world's own small OS, and Linux needs it
steps.body:
OP-TEE is a trusted operating system running at S-EL1 (the secure-world kernel level) in 32 MiB of DDR at `0x82000000`. It hosts trusted applications and secure keys, and owns the firewall setup.

On this SoC it is also the SCMI server (SCMI is Arm's message protocol for asking a platform to manage clocks and resets): Linux asks it for its clocks. Without OP-TEE the kernel cannot get them.

steps.title: U-Boot is the normal-world bootloader that finds Linux
steps.body:
U-Boot is loaded by BL2 to DDR `0x84000000` and starts at non-secure EL1, then relocates itself. It scans the bootable partition, reads `/boot/extlinux/extlinux.conf`, loads `Image` and the DTB (the device tree, the file describing the hardware) and runs `booti`.

It is built from the `u-boot` tree and packed into `fip.bin` as `u-boot-nodtb.bin`.

steps.title: Linux takes over and finishes the job
steps.body:
The kernel is loaded to `0x8a000000` (`kernel_addr_r`). It asks OP-TEE for clocks, mounts the root filesystem by PARTUUID (the unique ID of a GPT partition), runs `/sbin/init` and gives a serial login on `ttySTM0`.

It comes from the `linux-6.18.58` tarball and produces `Image`, the DTB and the root filesystem.

steps.title: Three hand-offs explain the whole chain
steps.body:
ROM to BL2: the ROM copies BL2 from `fsbla1` and jumps to it. BL2 is built with `RESET_TO_BL2`, so it runs at EL3 straight after the ROM.

BL2 to the rest: it finds the FIP by partition TYPE GUID `19d5df83-…` or by the name `fip`. BL31 to OP-TEE to U-Boot: BL31 runs OP-TEE once so it can initialise and serve SCMI, gets control back, then does an ERET (exception return) to U-Boot at non-secure EL1 (`STM32MP_BL33_EL1=1`).

anchor: Boot ROM, BL2: finished (SYSRAM is reused)
steps.title: Only BL31 and OP-TEE outlive the boot
steps.body:
Once Linux runs, the Boot ROM and BL2 are finished and their SYSRAM is reused. U-Boot is gone after `booti`.

BL31 stays at EL3 for good, serving every SMC and PSCI from SYSRAM. OP-TEE stays at S-EL1, reached through BL31, serving SCMI (clocks, resets) and trusted applications. That is why the secure world keeps affecting a running system.

steps.anchor: Power-on to login prompt: each stage loads the next. BL31 and OP-TEE stay resident after Linux is up.
steps.title: Takeaway: a chain that ends with two stages still running
steps.body:
Power-on to login prompt is six links, each one preparing the next. Four of them run in the secure world, and two of those stay alive beside Linux.

The address footnote at the bottom of the diagram names the source file for every address, so each claim can be checked.
